name: Google BigQuery
summary: Google Cloud’s serverless data warehouse: no clusters, and you pay per TiB scanned or per slot-hour.
intro: BigQuery stores each column separately, in its Capacitor format, and keeps storage and compute apart so each scales on its own. A query is split across many workers that scan only the columns it names. Compute is measured in slots, units of processing that Google assigns to each query from a large shared pool. There are no clusters to create: you load or stream data in and query it with GoogleSQL.

On demand, queries cost $6.25 per TiB scanned, the first TiB each month is free, and every query is billed for at least 10 MB. Steady workloads can buy capacity instead, as slot-hours in BigQuery editions. Through BigLake, BigQuery also queries Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi tables in Cloud Storage and other clouds, and BigQuery tables for Apache Iceberg keep data as Parquet in your own bucket while supporting full DML and streaming writes.
strengths: Truly serverless: nothing to size, and an on-demand project can use up to 2,000 slots at once
A free tier of 1 TiB of queries per month
Streaming ingest, partitioning and clustering, with SQL-based machine learning built in
Open formats through BigLake and managed Iceberg tables
limits: On-demand cost tracks bytes scanned: `SELECT *` on a wide, unpartitioned table can cost far more than expected
On tables that aren’t clustered, `LIMIT` doesn’t reduce the bytes a query scans; filters on partition and cluster columns do
GoogleSQL and native storage tie you to Google Cloud, so leaving means rewriting jobs
Delta Lake tables are read through BigLake; BigQuery can’t change their schema

story: In the mid-2000s, Google processed huge datasets with MapReduce, writing jobs in C++ or the Sawzall language. The conventional wisdom inside the company was “SQL doesn’t scale”, and Google had moved away from SQL almost completely. Commercial warehouses such as Teradata and Netezza ran on dedicated servers. Google wanted thousands of employees to ask ad-hoc questions of trillion-row datasets and get answers in seconds.

Dremel began in 2006 as a “20 percent” project by Andrey Gubarev. It stored data in columns, used a new encoding for the deeply nested Protocol Buffer records Google used for nearly all its data, and fanned each query out across a tree of servers. The 2010 VLDB paper by Sergey Melnik and colleagues described aggregation queries over trillion-row tables finishing in seconds. That same year, on the first day of Google I/O in May, Google introduced BigQuery: Dremel, offered to the public as a cloud service.

Dremel’s ideas spread well beyond Google. Apache Parquet, announced by Twitter and Cloudera in 2013, adopted its nested-column encoding, and separating storage from compute became the standard design for cloud warehouses.

choices.why: Early Dremel kept data on its own servers’ disks, so scaling storage meant adding CPUs too, and the data could only be read through Dremel. From 2009 Google moved it onto its shared file system, GFS, so compute and storage could scale separately.

choices.choice: Multi-tenant and serverless from the start
choices.why: Serving thousands of users interactively at low cost was only possible with one shared, multi-tenant pool and on-demand resources, rather than a cluster per user. Work was scheduled in abstract units called slots, still how BigQuery measures compute today.

Google’s logs had thousands of nested and repeated fields. Encoding them in columns let a query read only the fields it touched, and denormalised nested records avoided costly joins (Dremel had no joins at first).

choices.choice: Managed storage alongside querying files in place
choices.why: Querying raw files gave no chance to optimise layout, collect statistics or run updates and deletes, so BigQuery added its own managed storage while keeping external tables over open files.
